questions.lo: Elements and their physical and chemical properties
options: A substance made of only one type of atom
A mixture of two or more substances
Any substance that dissolves in water
A substance that is always a liquid
questions.explain: An element contains only one type of atom and cannot be broken down into simpler substances by a chemical reaction. Mixtures and compounds contain more than one type of atom.

questions.lo: Elements and their physical and chemical properties
questions.q: Which of these is a physical property of an element?
questions.explain: Physical properties (like melting point, density and conductivity) describe the substance itself. How it reacts with acids, oxygen or water are chemical properties.

questions.lo: Elements and their physical and chemical properties
questions.q: The chemical symbol for sodium is written correctly as:
questions.explain: A chemical symbol has a capital first letter and, if there is a second letter, it is lower case. So sodium is 'Na', not 'NA' or 'na'.

questions.lo: The principles behind Mendeleev's periodic table
questions.q: In 1869, how did Mendeleev arrange the elements in his periodic table?
options: In alphabetical order of their names
By atomic mass, lining up elements with similar properties
In the order they were discovered
questions.explain: Mendeleev ordered elements by atomic mass and placed elements with similar properties in the same columns, revealing a repeating pattern.

questions.lo: The principles behind Mendeleev's periodic table
questions.q: Why did Mendeleev leave gaps in his periodic table?
options: Because he had run out of space
For elements that had not yet been discovered
questions.explain: Mendeleev trusted the pattern of properties, so he left gaps for elements not yet discovered and even predicted their properties — predictions later shown to be correct.

questions.lo: The principles behind Mendeleev's periodic table
questions.q: What made Mendeleev's predictions so impressive to other scientists?
options: He invented all the elements himself
The properties of later-discovered elements matched his predictions
He proved elements do not really exist
He arranged the table by colour
questions.explain: When elements such as germanium were later discovered, their properties closely matched what Mendeleev had predicted from the gaps in his table — strong evidence that the pattern was real.

questions.lo: Groups and periods in the periodic table
questions.q: In the periodic table, a group is a:
questions.explain: A group is a vertical column. Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties. A horizontal row is called a period.

questions.lo: Groups and periods in the periodic table
questions.q: In the periodic table, a period is a:
questions.explain: A period is a horizontal row that goes across the table. Do not confuse it with a group, which is a vertical column.

questions.lo: Groups and periods in the periodic table
questions.q: Two elements are in the same group. What is most likely to be true about them?
options: They have very similar chemical properties
They are always in the same state (all gases)
They have exactly the same atomic mass
questions.explain: Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell.

questions.q: Where are most of the metals found in the periodic table?
options: On the left and in the middle
questions.explain: Most elements are metals, and they occupy the left and middle of the table. The non-metals sit in the top-right corner.

questions.q: Which set of properties best describes a typical metal?
options: Dull, brittle and a poor conductor
Shiny, bendy and a good conductor of electricity
Always a gas at room temperature
questions.explain: Typical metals are shiny, malleable (bendy) and good conductors of heat and electricity, with high melting points. Dull, brittle, poor conductors describe non-metals.

questions.q: An element is dull, does not conduct electricity, and is a gas at room temperature. It is most likely a:
questions.explain: Being dull, a poor conductor and a gas are all typical non-metal properties. Metals are shiny, good conductors and mostly solids.

questions.lo: Predicting reaction patterns using groups (Group 1, Group 7, Group 0)
questions.q: What happens to a Group 1 alkali metal when it reacts with water?
options: It fizzes and makes an alkaline solution plus hydrogen gas
It turns into a noble gas
questions.explain: Group 1 metals react with water, fizzing as they release hydrogen gas and forming an alkaline solution — which is why they are called alkali metals.

questions.lo: Predicting reaction patterns using groups (Group 1, Group 7, Group 0)
questions.q: Lithium, sodium and potassium are all in Group 1. Which reacts most violently with water?
questions.explain: Reactivity increases going down Group 1. Potassium is the lowest of the three, so it reacts most violently.

questions.lo: Predicting reaction patterns using groups (Group 1, Group 7, Group 0)
questions.q: Caesium is below potassium in Group 1. How would you predict caesium reacts with water?
options: It would not react at all
The same as a noble gas
questions.explain: Because reactivity increases down Group 1 and caesium is below potassium, we predict caesium reacts even more violently than potassium.

questions.lo: Predicting reaction patterns using groups (Group 1, Group 7, Group 0)
questions.q: In Group 7 (the halogens), how does reactivity change as you go down the group?
questions.explain: Group 7 is the opposite of Group 1: reactivity decreases going down the group, so chlorine (near the top) is more reactive than iodine (lower down).

questions.lo: Predicting reaction patterns using groups (Group 1, Group 7, Group 0)
questions.q: Astatine is at the bottom of Group 7, below iodine. What can you predict about its reactivity?
options: It is more reactive than fluorine
It is less reactive than iodine
questions.explain: Reactivity decreases down Group 7, so an element below iodine, like astatine, is predicted to be less reactive than iodine.

questions.lo: Predicting reaction patterns using groups (Group 1, Group 7, Group 0)
questions.q: Why are the Group 0 noble gases (such as helium and argon) so unreactive?
options: They have a full outer shell of electrons
questions.explain: Noble gases have a full outer shell of electrons, so they are stable and do not easily react — which is why they are described as inert.
